title: If we lived forever
translation: If the dew on the graves at Adashino never dried, if the smoke from the pyres at Toribeyama never cleared, if we just went on living forever, nothing would ever move us. The world is wonderful because nothing in it lasts.

Look at anything alive: nothing lives as long as we do. Mayflies are gone by evening. Summer cicadas never see spring or autumn. Even one year, if you really live it, is a long, easy stretch of time. But if you never feel you've had enough, a thousand years would go by like one night's dream.
We can't stay here forever anyway, so why hang on until we're ugly? The longer you live, the more you embarrass yourself. Before forty, at the latest: that's a decent time to go.

After that, people stop being embarrassed about how they look. They want to be out and about with everyone. In the evening of their lives they fuss over their grandchildren and want to live long enough to see them do well. All that's left is a greedy grip on the world, and they stop feeling anything for the beauty of things. It's pathetic.

literal: If the dew of Adashino never vanished and the smoke of Toribeyama never cleared, and it were the rule that we lived on to the end (forever), how utterly without feeling for things it would be!
The world: its being uncertain is exactly what is splendid.
When you look at things that have life, none is as long-lived as humans.
There are mayflies that wait (only) for evening, and summer cicadas that do not know spring and autumn.
Even the time of spending one year attentively is incomparably leisurely.
If you think 'not enough, it's a pity', then even if you spend a thousand years, it will surely feel like the dream of one night.
In a world where you cannot live forever, what will you do by waiting until you have an ugly form?
If life is long, shames are many.
Even at the longest, dying at an age short of forty is surely what is seemly.

Once that age has passed, without a heart ashamed of one's looks, one thinks of going out to mix with people, loves one's descendants in the evening sun, hopes for a life long enough to see their prosperous future, only the heart that greedily clings to the world grows deep, and one comes not to know the feeling of things: that is wretched.

notes.text: Adashino and Toribeyama were burial and cremation grounds outside Kyoto. So 'the dew of Adashino' and 'the smoke of Toribeyama' mean graves and funerals. A reader in 1330 sees death in the first line, before the sentence even says 'if we lived forever'. あだし itself means 'fleeting, vain', which suits the place.
さらで: {去|さ}る 'to go away' + で 'without': 'never going away'.

notes.quote: いかに物の哀れもなからむ
notes.text: {物|もの}の{哀|あは}れ, mono no aware: the feeling that things move you, often with sadness because they pass. Kenkō's point is that this feeling needs impermanence.

notes.quote: 世は定めなきこそいみじけれ
notes.text: The key sentence. こそ … けれ again, as in the preface: いみじ becomes いみじけれ. いみじ is a strong word in both directions, 'terrible' or 'wonderful'. Here it is the good direction, and that is the surprise.
The mayfly that lives only until evening is an old image from Chinese texts. The 1925 edition notes the Huainanzi: the mayfly 'is born in the morning and dies in the evening'.
Also borrowed, and the 1925 edition gives the source: Zhuangzi, 壽則多辱, 'long life, much disgrace'. Educated readers would recognise the line.

notes.quote: 四十に足らぬほどにて死なむこそ
notes.text: Kenkō was born around 1283, and he probably wrote most of the book around 1330, in his late forties. So he was already past his own deadline when he wrote this. He went on to live to about seventy. {四十|よそぢ}: ぢ counts decades of life, as in みそぢ 'thirty'.
めやすし 'easy on the eyes, decent'. こそ … べけれ: the realis form of べし closes the こそ.
'In the evening sun', meaning old age. This echoes a line by the Chinese poet Bai Juyi about old officials who will not retire: 'in the evening sun they worry about their descendants' (夕陽憂子孫).
Another {係|かか}り{結|むす}び, of a different kind: なむ needs the attributive form ({連体形|れんたいけい}) at the end, so あさまし becomes あさましき. Compare こそ, which needs the realis form.
